author: reek
body: Bare-metal VMX hypervisor. Creates a guest VM using Intel VT-x and runs a Codex CDX binary inside it. VM exits for I/O ports are dispatched to Codex device model functions. This replaces QEMU -- Codex is its own hypervisor.

author: reek
body: So the gate belongs here too, and it answers zero rather than faulting. A revision id of zero is never valid, and the two callers that matter both refuse before they would use it.

author: reek
body: The general shape, since this is the third function in this chapter to need it: reading a VMX MSR is itself a VMX operation. Everything in this file that touches one has to ask whether the processor is in a state where that is legal, and none of them did.

author: reek
body: The VMX capability MSRs (IA32_VMX_PINBASED_CTLS and its neighbours) are the same class as IA32_VMX_BASIC above: they exist only on a processor with VMX enabled and are a #GP anywhere else. Without the gate this faults at the same instruction, which is what `vmx-launch-test` and `vmx-serial-test` did.

author: reek
body: With no capability MSR to consult there is nothing to adjust, so the desired control word comes back untouched. That value is never used -- both lifecycle entries refuse first -- and returning it rather than zero keeps this a pure clamp rather than a second, quieter failure signal.

author: reek
body: **`vmx-enable` used to return `VmxOk` unconditionally**, discarding the result of `vmxon`, and `VmxFailed` was declared and never constructed anywhere in the tree. On a machine without VT-x that is not a wrong answer so much as no answer: the caller is told the processor entered VMX operation, proceeds to `vmwrite`, and dies. `codex/test/apps/vmx-init-test` asserted `vmx-enable:ok` against it, which is a test that could not fail, behind a skip that claimed it needed real hardware.

author: reek
body: `vmxon` cannot be asked. The runtime helper is `F3 0F C7 37` followed by `ret` and never reads RFLAGS, so its return value is whatever RAX happened to hold; the instruction reports through CF and ZF and nothing carries them back. So availability is established BEFORE the instruction rather than inferred after it.

author: reek
body: IA32_FEATURE_CONTROL is the authority, and it is the same one every hypervisor uses. Bit 0 is the lock: the firmware sets it once and the MSR is read-only afterwards. Bit 2 enables VMX outside SMX. VMXON raises #GP unless the lock is set AND that enable bit is set, so both must be true and nothing else needs asking.

author: reek
body: A sentence a human can act on. "VMX unavailable" tells an operator nothing; "enable VT-x in the firmware" tells them where to go.

author: reek
body: The VMCS operations are meaningless outside VMX operation -- `vmclear` and `vmptrld` raise #UD when the processor never entered it -- so this refuses for the same reason and by the same test rather than running them and returning OK regardless.

author: val
body: IA32_VMX_BASIC EXISTS ONLY ON A PROCESSOR IN WHICH VMX IS ENABLED, and reading it anywhere else is a #GP, not a zero. Measured: this faulted with `!EXC=0d RIP=... RDI=0000000000000480` under codex-vm -- 0x480 being the MSR index -- before any of the availability checks below could run, because a caller naturally asks for the revision id first and hands it to `vmx-enable`.

author: val
body: **Measured here rather than assumed** (2026-07-27, under codex-vm): the MSR reads **1** -- lock set, VMX-outside-SMX clear -- which is exactly the encoding of a machine whose firmware has VT-x turned off. It is not zero, which is what the "an MSR outside codex-vm's list reads zero" note would have predicted, and the difference is worth having measured: the conclusion is the same and the reason for it is not.

author: val
body: Intel's encoding, not ours (SDM Vol 3C, 29.3.2 and 29.4.2). In an EPT entry that maps a 2 MB page, bits 2:0 are read, write and execute, bits 5:3 carry the EPT memory type, and bit 7 marks the entry as a leaf rather than a pointer to the next table; the frame occupies bits 51:21. A non-leaf entry carries the permission bits and the next table's address and nothing else. The EPT pointer holds the memory type in bits 2:0 and the page-walk length MINUS ONE in bits 5:3, so a four-level walk is written as three.

author: val
body: A raw CDX guest enters at `__start`, which loads RSP from `ram-size-addr` and then stores its heap position to `deck-pos-addr`, both absolute addresses inside the first 64 KB. Under EPT those are guest-physical, so they land in this freshly allocated region rather than in the host's low memory, and the region is handed over unzeroed: zeroing the whole guest would be one store per dword across the entire allocation. Only the low window is initialised, and the RAM size the guest will adopt as its stack top is written there.
